headline: New Moon Springs Load The Race — Bonito Show Early Off Fishers Island
subhead: Big tides and sunset stripers converge this weekend while the fluke bail out of the bay and the first Spanish mackerel show up on cold-wall collapse.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does before a new moon — it built. Wind stayed out of the northeast for most of the stretch, which kept the surface chop honest but also sharpened the thermal breaks along the 20-30 fathom edges east of us, the same upwelling that's been stacking bluefin farther out on the Coimbra corridor. Closer to home, that NE flow did something else useful: it kept cooler water pinned against the Fishers Island shoreline while the bay side of Gardiners and Peconic pushed past 78 degrees. That temperature split is the whole story of the week — bait and predators both reacting to it, just in different directions.

This week the moon takes over. New moon lands right in this window, which means spring tides building through Friday and peaking Saturday into Monday, July 11-13. Bigger tidal range means harder current through The Race and Plum Gut — I'm talking 4 to 5 knots at max ebb off Little Gull — and it also means the evening flood is now stacking up right against sunset. That's the first PM flood-sunset alignment we've had since the June full moon, and it's the window I'd build a whole trip around. When the flood peaks right at last light, bass push up onto the structure to feed on the push instead of just riding the current lane, and that's when the big fish show themselves in the white water.

Bass fishing through Plum Gut and The Race has been real but not automatic — I've had two-fish nights and skunk nights in the same 72 hours, which tells you it's tide-dependent, not a blanket bite. The pattern that's working: fish the last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of high, right in the rip line off Orient Point Light and along the north side of Plum Gut where the eddy forms behind the reef. Eels are still the closer after dark — an 8 to 10-inch snake fished on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that current, dead-drifted through the seam where the fast water meets the slower back-eddy. During the day, bucktails in the 2 to 3-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked with a slow lift-drop through the same eddy pockets have put 28 to 34-inch fish in the boat. Nothing over 40 this week that I've seen personally, though there's chatter of bigger fish scattered from here out toward Block Island and the Cape — pockets, not a run. I'd treat any 40-plus as a bonus, not an expectation, until this new moon push proves it can hold bigger bass on the structure consistently.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player. Slammers in the 8 to 12-pound class are hitting hard on the same tide stages as the bass, but they're less picky about exact timing — anywhere from mid-incoming through the top of the tide off Fishers Island Race and the rip line running north of Race Rock has produced. Diamond jigs, 2 to 4 ounces, worked with a fast erratic retrieve through the moving water is still the ticket, and if you want top-water violence, a big Danny-style swimmer over the same structure at first light will get hit.

Fluke have officially left the bay. That 78.8-degree water in Gardiners and the upper bay pushed them hard into the channels and out toward the inlets, and the upwelled 71-degree water on the ocean side of Plum Gut and around Orient Point is exactly where they've relocated. The play now is outgoing tide, working the channel edges in 25 to 40 feet with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom as the current empties out through the Gut. Fish to 5 pounds have come from that stretch this week, with better numbers than size — a lot of 16 to 18-inch shorts mixed in, so you're sorting through fish to find keepers, but they're there in numbers worth the drift time.

The development I'm watching closest is the bonito. The cold wall that's normally sitting between Block Island and Rhode Island Sound collapsed hard — better than 10 degrees warmer than it was — and that's opened a corridor for bonito and Spanish mackerel to spread west from Point Judith toward us. First reports of Spanish showing on the ocean side of the inlets out east of Montauk this week fit right into that pattern, and Fishers Island Race, with its clean incoming water and structure, is exactly the kind of spot that corridor could reach next. If you're rigged for it — small Deadly Dick or Kastmaster in the 1-ounce range, worked fast on light tackle — I'd keep a rod ready any time you're running past the Race in the middle of the day. It's not a sure thing yet, but the water's right and the fish are moving in this direction.

Weakfish, for the record, are still a non-event. Water's been above 70 for over two weeks now and I haven't heard of a single fish, which tells you temperature alone isn't the trigger people hoped it was — I wouldn't burn a tide on them right now.

If I had one shot this weekend, I'd take the Saturday evening flood at Plum Gut, eel in hand, timed to hit max current right as the sun drops. That's the best alignment we've had all month. Backup plan if the bass go quiet: swing over to the fluke grounds on the ebb and salvage the trip with bucktails on the bottom.
